intro: Deciding when and where to take a picture can matter as much as the camera. Compare the face in a quiet study, a moving crowd, colored light and a deliberately ordered workplace.
alt: Black-and-white studio photograph, a busy street photograph, a colorful reflected-light portrait and a distant frontal workplace photograph.

variants.name: straight photography
variants.look: Precise focus and side light give the subject clear edges and controlled gray values.
variants.history: Early-20th-century photographers such as Paul Strand explored photography’s ability to describe forms directly through sharp detail and tone.
variants.when: Make a study of the way window light falls across the face or an object.
variants.why: Clarity directs attention to the form and light already present in front of the camera.

variants.name: street photography
variants.look: The subject is caught in mid-step among layered people and surroundings.
variants.history: Smaller handheld cameras helped make the unscripted public scene a major subject in 20th-century photography. Helen Levitt photographed street life in New York.
variants.when: Show how a character moves through a shared public space.
variants.why: An unrepeatable combination of gestures and surroundings gives the moment its energy.

variants.name: color photography
variants.look: Cyan reflections and orange light shape the face and surroundings.
variants.history: William Eggleston's color photographs helped establish a place for color in American fine-art photography in the 1970s.
variants.when: Make the particular colors of an ordinary moment carry the picture.
variants.why: The relationship between colors helps place the subject and can establish a distinctive mood.

variants.name: Düsseldorf School photography
variants.look: A frontal, detached view lets the workplace grid occupy as much attention as the figure.
variants.history: Bernd and Hilla Becher taught at the Düsseldorf art academy and developed systematic series of industrial structures. Several of their students explored highly detailed large-scale photographs.
variants.when: Compare different people or offices using the same camera height and framing.
variants.why: A consistent viewpoint makes small differences easier to notice.

prompt: Create one square atlas comparison plate, precisely four independently composed equally sized artwork squares in full-bleed 2x2 grid, hard splits on both midlines, no margin nor gutter. Present the heroine as a real photographed person. In all scenes a mug is visible. Use the attached illustration only as subject character reference. 30-year-old attractive ash-blonde woman with tidy low bun, black rectangular eyeglasses clearly visible in every panel, tailored charcoal knee-length business dress under fitted blazer, signature white coffee mug with small four-color windowpane mark and plain blue lanyard with a blank badge. Never reproduce the card border or typography. The artwork techniques differ dramatically. Put nothing that crosses the splits. No letters, words, numerals or panel labels anywhere. TOP LEFT: straight photography, precisely focused gelatin-silver black-and-white side light catches glasses and a precise study of quiet tones. TOP RIGHT: candid street photograph, she passes through a layered crowd near an office cafe, captured mid-step with photographic grain. BOTTOM LEFT: large luscious direct color photograph, pale blue morning light balanced with saturated cyan and orange-red window reflections, deliberate chromatic composition. BOTTOM RIGHT: Düsseldorf School-inspired neutral high-resolution frontal typological color view of subject at workplace, minimal industrial grid and flat daylight from distant viewpoint.
